questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the camera took over from painting
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish what the camera inherited from painting from what it displaced
questions.stem: Your design brief for a gallery label must explain what the camera took over from painting, and your first draft claims the photograph simply replaced the painted portrait.

options.text: Photography inherited painting's task of fixing a likeness and standing for a particular person.
Photography took over painting's role as a commissioned object displayed for wealthy buyers.
options.misconception: confuses patronage history with technical change

options.text: Photography inherited painting's method of passing workshop practice down by apprenticeship.
options.misconception: believes technique transmission explains technological change

options.text: Photography took over painting's function as a devotional picture for shared religious rooms.
options.misconception: assumes every early photograph served devotional use

questions.explanation: The camera inherited painting's claim to fix a particular likeness. Patronage, workshop training and devotional use belong to other histories, so crediting them to the handover misdescribes the change.
questions.hint: Think about what the painted portrait promised the viewer.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What indexicality does and does not license
questions.learningObjective: State which claims an indexical photograph supports and which it does not
questions.stem: Writing museum kiosk copy, you decide how to describe what a photograph guarantees, and your draft says every photograph is direct evidence of the truth of its caption.

options.text: Only the light that reached the emulsion is guaranteed, so captions must be checked against other evidence.
A photograph guarantees the truth of whatever caption is printed beside it.
options.misconception: treats the index as a guarantee of meaning

options.text: A photograph guarantees that nothing was staged, framed or cropped before it was taken.
options.misconception: assumes the frame is always unedited reality

options.text: A photograph guarantees the identity of every person who appears in it.
options.misconception: confuses appearance with identification

questions.explanation: A photograph is causally linked to its subject, so it supports claims about what stood before the lens. It cannot certify meaning, staging or identity, which depend on captioning and selection.
questions.hint: Ask what physically had to happen for the image to exist.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The limits of indexicality as testimony
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a trace of light does not amount to testimony
questions.stem: Drafting the interpretation panel for a wall about surveillance photographs, you must explain why a trace of light is not the same as testimony.

answer.exemplar: A photograph bears a causal trace of what was in front of the lens, so it testifies that something was there at a moment and to its optical appearance. It does not testify to what that something meant, what participants intended, or what an archivist's caption asserts. Those require corroboration from documents, records and context, and the image alone cannot settle them.

questions.explanation: Indexicality guarantees a causal link to the referent, not a reading of it. The panel should separate what the image can evidence from what the caption and context add.
questions.hint: Separate physical contact with the referent from meaning.

questions.explanation: Inspection rejects 45 copies, since 250 times 0.18 is 45, leaving 205 that can circulate. Conceptually the same point holds: value shifts from the unique object toward the reproducible edition.
questions.hint: Work out the rejected number, then subtract.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a manifesto is for
questions.learningObjective: Identify the function of a founding text addressed to a public

stimulus.body: The sheet announces a programme: a list of demands addressed to anyone who makes images, a refusal of a named standard, and a date by which readers should respond. It is printed cheaply and circulated by post and by hand.

questions.stem: The scanning rig's operator manual mentions a printed sheet circulated among image-makers, and you need to explain what such a sheet is for.

options.text: It is a public announcement of a programme and a demand addressed to a public.
It is a private record of the artist's working method for studio assistants.
options.misconception: treats the manifesto as private documentation

options.text: It is a technical specification for materials that readers are required to buy.
options.misconception: reads the manifesto as a materials order form

options.text: It is a retrospective summary of a movement's history written years after it began.
options.misconception: confuses a call to action with a later history

questions.explanation: A manifesto is a public bid for attention that declares a programme and expects readers to act. Reading it as private documentation, a purchase list or a later history misses that function.
questions.hint: Ask who is addressed and what they are meant to do.

questions.topic: Refusing the gallery system
questions.learningObjective: Separate the two benefits sought when the gallery is refused
questions.stem: Your conservation imaging brief asks why an artist might stage a show in a disused tram depot rather than a commercial gallery, and your note must separate the two benefits involved.

options.text: It reaches audiences the gallery's gatekeeping excludes, and it sets the terms of the encounter outside the market.
It guarantees a higher sale price, and it gives the artist more control over the lighting.
options.misconception: assumes a non-gallery venue improves both price and conditions

options.text: It removes the need for documentation, and it shortens the artist's working hours.
options.misconception: believes refusing the gallery removes documentation duties

options.text: It makes the work easier to insure, and it lowers the cost of the artist's materials.
options.misconception: thinks venue choice mainly changes insurance and materials

questions.explanation: Two gains are at stake: reaching an audience commercial gatekeeping excludes, and setting display terms outside market pressure. Neither concerns price, paperwork or materials, so options bundling those mislead.
questions.hint: Separate audience access from control of the encounter.

questions.topic: A critique made from inside the market
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a critique can operate within the commercial system it attacks
questions.stem: Photographing an empty gallery wall for a catalogue, you notice the artist has priced work at market rate while writing a text criticising the market.

options.text: The critique works by using the market's own terms to expose the system it operates in.
The critique fails because any work sold through a gallery has left criticism behind.
options.misconception: believes any market participation ends criticism

options.text: The critique succeeds only if the gallery removes the artist's name from the price list.
options.misconception: thinks critique depends on the dealer withdrawing support

options.text: The critique is strongest when the artist sells the work privately at a lower price.
options.misconception: assumes undercutting the price strengthens the argument

questions.explanation: A critique from inside the market borrows the market's authority and lets it expose its own logic. Pricing at market rate beside critical text does exactly that, so the sale does not cancel the critique.
questions.hint: Ask where the artist's contradiction is located.

Paintings remain the larger group, so photography has never taken over any of painting's functions.

options.text: The collection proves that painting and photography do different jobs with no overlap at all.
options.misconception: mistakes separate categories for a complete absence of overlap

options.text: The counts show that photographs were collected mainly for technical experiment rather than for content.
options.misconception: attributes collecting motive to medium without evidence

questions.explanation: Photographs outnumber paintings in the accession book, showing camera-made records now doing work painting once did. Proportions alone cannot prove motive, exclusivity or complete takeover.
questions.hint: Read the ratio without over-claiming its cause.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What indexicality does and does not license
questions.learningObjective: Set out what a photograph can and cannot establish about its subject
questions.stem: A print shop's contract for facsimile panels asks you to state, in your own words, what a photograph can and cannot establish about its subject.

answer.exemplar: A photograph is causally linked to its subject by the light that reaches the film, so it supports claims that the subject existed, that it appeared in a particular way, and that the exposure occurred at a particular moment. It does not support claims about the subject's meaning, the photographer's intention, the truth of a caption, or the completeness of the frame, all of which depend on context and corroboration.

questions.explanation: Indexicality licenses claims about existence, appearance at the moment of exposure, and timing. Everything about meaning, intention and caption truth needs other evidence.
questions.hint: Ask what physically had to occur for the image.

questions.hint: Multiply the retained share by the number of frames.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What mechanical reproduction does to originality
questions.learningObjective: Identify where variation moves when several prints share one negative

stimulus.body: Three prints from the same negative are catalogued with different captions: a market stall, a market stall on a market day, and a market on a Tuesday. The negative bears one set of scratches and no visible retouching.

questions.stem: Captioning the survey photographs for the archive, you meet three prints from one negative carrying three different captions, and you must explain what the copies share.

options.text: They share one image, so the differences lie in interpretation, captioning and use rather than in the picture itself.
They show three different moments, because a single negative can hold several exposures.
options.misconception: believes one negative can record several distinct moments

options.text: They are three separate originals, and the shared scratches are a coincidence of handling.
options.misconception: treats shared plate marks as evidence of coincidence

options.text: They differ in originality, since each print counts as an independent work of art.
options.misconception: confuses physical copies with distinct authored works

questions.explanation: All three prints derive from one negative, so the image is fixed while captions, dates and uses vary. Reproduction shifts variation out of the picture into the caption and the market around it.
questions.hint: Separate what the negative fixes from what the caption adds.

questions.stem: Two engineers argue about whether the sheet of demands you are typesetting for a group of image-makers is a manifesto, and you must separate its function from its form.

It is a manifesto because it reproduces the hand of the artist who wrote it.
options.misconception: thinks authority of handwriting makes a document a manifesto

options.text: It is a manifesto because it was printed in multiple copies rather than written once.

options.text: It is a manifesto because it records the finished state of an already existing style.
options.misconception: confuses a declaration of intent with a record of style

questions.explanation: A manifesto is defined by what it does: it states a programme, a refusal and an expectation that readers respond. Form, print run and handwriting are not what make it one, so those grounds miss the point.
questions.hint: Test the document by its declared purpose.

questions.stem: The exhibition's lighting designer needs a label explaining why an artist hung work in stairwells and underpasses rather than in a gallery.

Such a work is by definition a commercial advertisement paid for by the artist.
options.misconception: confuses site-specific work with commercial promotion

options.text: Such a work avoids the need for a curator because anyone may rearrange it freely.

options.text: Such a work exists mainly because public spaces have better lighting than galleries.
options.misconception: reduces the choice of site to lighting quality alone

questions.explanation: Refusing the gallery changes where and to whom the work is addressed, reaching beyond gallery-goers. It does not turn the work into advertising, remove authorship, or rest on lighting quality.
questions.hint: Think about who the work is addressed to.

questions.stem: Working out what a curator's label should say, you review a ledger: 60 works sold through a commercial gallery, 14 of them with critical essays, and 11 whose prices rose after the essays ran. What does the ledger support?

options.text: Criticism circulated inside the commercial system can affect value, which is why such critique is absorbed.
The ledger proves that critics decided every price rise in the gallery's history.
options.misconception: treats correlation as proof of single cause

options.text: The ledger shows that only untethered works by unknown artists ever attract critical writing.
options.misconception: generalises from eleven cases to all artists

questions.explanation: Criticism and price movement appear together inside the market, showing the system can absorb critique. One ledger cannot show critics caused every rise or that all cases resemble these eleven.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the camera took over from painting
questions.learningObjective: Describe the handover from painted likeness to recorded likeness
questions.stem: The framing jig you are designing is for a display that pairs an early painted portrait with a photograph of the same sitter, and the text must explain the handover.

answer.exemplar: The camera took over from painting the task of fixing a likeness and of claiming to record a particular person's presence at a particular time. Painting did not lose its role entirely, and it kept its labour, scale and materials, but portraiture and documentary record increasingly passed to the camera, which could produce many likenesses instead of one hand-made object.

questions.explanation: The handover concerned the task of recording likeness, not patronage, materials or technique. A label that says photography simply replaced painting loses the differences in labour and use.
questions.hint: Ask which function migrated, not which institution did.

options.text: It refused the gallery by relocating the encounter to where people already walk.
It refused the gallery by giving the work an infinite edition at no cost to the maker.
options.misconception: confuses refusal of the market with an attempt to price at zero

options.text: It refused the gallery by replacing the object with a durable printed substitute.

options.text: It refused the gallery by removing any dependence on weather or public space.
options.misconception: believes open-air display removes practical constraints on the work

questions.explanation: The refusal was spatial and social: the work met an audience on its daily path, not in a gallery. That changes reach and framing, not pricing, replica substitution or the demands of outdoor placement.
questions.hint: Focus on where and for whom the encounter happened.

questions.stem: In a review of the museum's signage, a caption claims that a photograph is proof its subjects were present, and you must separate the physical trace from the testimonial claim.

options.text: The image traces light from the scene, so it evidences presence of appearance, not truth of the account.
The image traces light from the scene, so it evidences every statement made in the caption.
options.misconception: mistakes a physical trace for confirmation of a caption

options.text: The image records nothing physical, so it evidences only what the curator later added.
options.misconception: denies the image any physical link to what was filmed

options.text: The image captures the photographer's intention, so it evidences what the scene was meant to show.
options.misconception: confuses the maker's intention with the scene's meaning

The reprint was made because the original text had been damaged and could not be read.
options.misconception: assumes republishing is always a conservation response

options.text: The reprint documented a completed movement so that later visitors could study its history.
options.misconception: confuses a programme statement with a retrospective account

options.text: The reprint listed prices so that visitors could judge the market value of the works.
options.misconception: reads a founding text as a price list for the market

questions.explanation: Reprinting a founding text for a new audience restates a programme and recruits participants. Damage, retrospective documentation and price listing would each give a different reason for the reprint.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the camera took over from painting
questions.learningObjective: Interpret identical measurement scores from two different source media
questions.stem: Comparing two image-processing pipelines, one team scanned 600 archival prints and another scanned 300 original negatives; both report the same fidelity score for every frame. What can be concluded?

options.text: Equal scores from prints and originals show the score measures the pipeline, not the physical source.
Equal scores prove that prints and negatives carry identical information.
options.misconception: treats a measurement score as proof of identity

options.text: Equal scores prove that scanning originals is unnecessary because prints lose nothing.
options.misconception: concludes source material is irrelevant from one metric

options.text: Equal scores show that the negatives were scanned incorrectly by the first team.
options.misconception: assumes an identical outcome must be an error

questions.explanation: A fidelity score that ignores the source cannot separate prints from negatives, so identical scores describe the pipeline only. They reveal nothing about whether the two sources hold the same information.
questions.hint: Ask what the score actually varies with.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A critique made from inside the market
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a critique operates while remaining inside the market
questions.stem: A residency brief asks you to write about an artist who sells through dealers while attacking the dealers' role, and the text must explain the strategy.

answer.exemplar: The artist works inside the commercial system and lets it operate on its own terms: prices follow the market, works are signed and dated, and the dealer handles the sale. The critical writing sits beside those concessions, so the system's own claims are what the audience is asked to judge. The strategy depends on staying inside the market, since refusal would remove the thing being examined.

questions.explanation: Working inside the market lets the artist use the system's own authority to expose it, which is why the sale and the critique coexist. Stepping outside would remove the very mechanism under examination.
questions.hint: Ask what the critique needs the market in order to do.

questions.learningObjective: Set out what refusing the gallery gains and what it costs
questions.stem: Drafting a wall text about early street-based shows, you must explain what the artist gained and what the artist gave up by refusing galleries.

answer.exemplar: Refusing the gallery moved the encounter into streets, stations and other public places, so the work met people who would not have sought it out and no longer depended on a dealer or a gatekeeper to be seen. questions.topic: What mechanical reproduction does to originality

answer.exemplar: The camera's indexical link is a physical and causal one: light from the scene fell on a photosensitive surface and altered it. A staged scene, a doctored print or a false caption leaves that link intact, so the resulting object is still a photograph and still bears a trace of what was in front of the lens. options.misconception: reads a minority answer as the dominant one

questions.explanation: The spread across source, edition and person shows originality redefined in several directions rather than abandoned. No single group, large or small, settles what the public now believes.
questions.hint: Compare the groups before concluding anything.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the camera took over from painting
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the handover changed the making of later work
questions.stem: Explaining why an artist's refusal to accept commissions changed the way later work was made, you must connect the change to what the camera had taken over.

answer.exemplar: Once the camera absorbed the task of producing a likeness, a painted portrait was no longer obliged to record a patron's face as proof of status. Painters were freed to spend the same labour on what a camera could not do, such as constructing a space, a mood or a point of view. The handover therefore did not end portraiture; it changed the terms on which portraiture could be painted, and later work inherited those terms.

questions.explanation: When likeness moved to the camera, painting could turn to what the camera could not do, so commissioned portraiture changed. The handover changed painting's terms rather than ending the genre.
questions.hint: Ask what painting could do once likeness left it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What indexicality does and does not license
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the number of exposures recorded by a timed rig
questions.stem: A rig fires two exposures each second for a continuous 180-second survey window; how many exposures does the camera record in total?
questions.explanation: Two exposures a second across 180 seconds gives 360 exposures. The count records light reaching the emulsion, which is what an image can testify to, and nothing about later claims made for it.
questions.hint: Multiply the rate by the duration.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What indexicality does and does not license
questions.learningObjective: Determine what cropping changes and what it preserves

stimulus.body: The log for a set of photographs records, for each frame, the shutter release, the lens fitted, the light condition and the time. It also records that eleven frames were later cropped for the printed catalogue, and the crops are noted separately from the unaltered negatives.

questions.stem: Reviewing an audit trail for photographs, you find that eleven frames were cropped for print while the negatives remained whole.

options.text: The negative preserves more of the scene than the print, so each is evidence of a different extent.
The crop proves the photographer staged the scene, since only staged scenes need trimming.
options.misconception: treats editing as proof of deliberate staging

options.text: The crop shows the image was faked, because altering a frame removes its indexical link.
options.misconception: believes cropping destroys the image's causal link

options.text: The crop shows the negative is the finished work, since the print is merely a copy of it.
options.misconception: assumes a negative is always a finished work

questions.explanation: The indexical link survives cropping, since the light reaching the emulsion is unchanged, but the extent of the record differs between negative and print. Editing changes what is shown, not the mechanism.
questions.hint: Ask what cropping changes and what it leaves.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What mechanical reproduction does to originality
questions.learningObjective: Separate the mechanical fact of copying from the claim to originality
questions.stem: Comparing two accounts of what makes a photograph original, you must separate the mechanical fact from the claim about status.

options.text: The mechanical fact is repeatable copying; the status claim is firstness, derivation or authentication.
The mechanical fact is repeatability; the status claim is that no two copies can ever be equal.
options.misconception: makes exclusivity of copies the basis of originality

options.text: The mechanical fact is that copies are degraded; the status claim is that only degradation proves originality.
options.misconception: treats degradation as the proof of an original status

options.text: The mechanical fact is that originals are singular; the status claim is that copies have no value.
options.misconception: confuses the price of copies with their status

questions.explanation: Mechanical reproduction means copies can repeat, so originality rests on claims about firstness, derivation or authentication rather than physical uniqueness. Singular form is one possible basis among several.
questions.hint: Separate the process from the status claim.
